title: Attention residue
hookLine: part of the mind stays on the last task after the switch (Leroy)

cards: The meeting ended ten minutes ago. The body has moved on: new room, new screen, new task. But a sentence from the meeting is still playing.
What did she mean by that? Should I have said something? The report in front of you gets read, and read again, and nothing goes in.
Part of the mind didn't get the memo that it moved. A researcher named Sophie Leroy gave that leftover a name, and it's today's word.

teach.b: First, the finding. Leroy studied what happens when people leave one task and start another.
Thoughts about the first task kept running in the background, and people with more of those leftover thoughts did worse on the next task.
She called it attention residue: some of your attention stays stuck to the thing you just left. Second, what makes it stickier.
In her studies, residue was stronger when the first task was left unfinished. A half-done job keeps tapping on the shoulder.
When people finished it, especially under a little time pressure that pushed them to close it out, the residue was lower. Third, a way to loosen it.

teach.h: WRITE WHERE YOU'LL PICK IT UP.
teach.b: In later work, Leroy and a colleague tested something simple: before switching, people wrote a quick plan for where they would pick the task back up.
That small note seemed to help the mind let go, as if it trusted the plan to remember so it didn't have to. Fourth, an old echo.
The Stoic emperor Marcus Aurelius, in his private notebook, kept urging himself to give full attention to the thing in hand and to set aside every other thought while doing it.
He had no lab and no word for residue, but he knew the problem: the mind trailing behind the body, still in the last room. The research doesn't say you can switch with no leftover.
It suggests the leftover can shrink, by finishing what you can and writing down what you can't.

how: People who use this research often close each task with a short note on where to resume, or take a brief pause between meetings before starting the next thing.

o: leftover clutter from a project, like old files
the part of the mind still stuck on the last task
the tiredness that builds up over a long workday

games.q: inside attention residue: tap the pairs.
p: attend to the thing in hand

s: once you change tasks, your attention moves with you
Leroy found thoughts about the last task keep running in the background.
residue was stronger when the first task was left unfinished
a half-done job kept more attention stuck to it.
the research says a perfect switch with no leftover is possible
it suggests the leftover can be made smaller, not that it disappears.

games.q: you have to leave a report half finished and jump into a meeting. what helps the residue most, by Leroy's later work?
o: promise yourself you'll stop thinking about it.
write a quick line on where you'll pick it back up.
keep the report open on a second screen.
games.why: a short plan for where to resume seemed to help the mind let go of the unfinished task.

practice: Bring back whatever you were doing just before this, and if it's unfinished, say silently in one short sentence where you'll pick it up: next I'll call the landlord, next I'll fix page three.
That's the note, so set it down and let the breath be the new room you've walked into. When the last task tugs, don't fight it; remind yourself the note has it, and come back.

wordCard.voice: Attention residue. The part of the mind that stays on the last task after you've moved to the next one. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: clear the residue. The note remembers, so the mind can let go. Same time tomorrow.
